flashcards.q: What is the single deciding question between server-side sessions and stateless JWTs?
flashcards.a: Revocation. Sessions can be invalidated instantly (delete the row); a stateless JWT is valid until it expires no matter what the server wants, because there is nothing to delete.

flashcards.q: Give the one-line mental model distinguishing a session from a token.
flashcards.a: A session is a pointer to truth (redirectable instantly); a token is a photocopy of truth, timestamped (valid until the timestamp says otherwise, no matter what).

flashcards.q: What is the production-standard hybrid pattern for token-based auth?
flashcards.a: Short-lived (5-15 min) stateless JWT access tokens for the hot path (zero-lookup verification), backed by a server-tracked, revocable opaque refresh token (DB row) used only to mint new access tokens.

flashcards.q: In the hybrid access/refresh token model, what bounds the worst-case exposure window after revocation?
flashcards.a: The access token's TTL, not the refresh token's lifetime -- revoking the refresh token stops new access tokens from being minted, but any already-issued access token remains valid until its own (short) expiry.

flashcards.q: What is the typical latency cost of a Redis session lookup versus a local JWT signature verification?
flashcards.a: Redis session lookup: ~0.5-2ms with a network round trip. Local JWT verification (HMAC or RSA): sub-0.5ms with zero network calls.

flashcards.q: Why is 'JWTs mean we don't need a database' a false claim?
flashcards.a: Authorization decisions (distinct from authentication) frequently need current state -- permissions can change between token issuance and use, and object-level checks require a lookup regardless of what's encoded in the token.

flashcards.q: Why does putting a JWT in a cookie vs an Authorization header change the security model, not just the transport?
flashcards.a: A cookie is auto-attached by the browser, reintroducing CSRF exposure (mitigated via SameSite + anti-CSRF tokens); a header-based Bearer token needs explicit JS to attach it, avoiding CSRF but requiring the token be JS-accessible, exposing it to XSS exfiltration if stored in localStorage.

flashcards.q: Why did the industry actually move toward tokens, precisely -- not the overstated version?
flashcards.a: Removing the network dependency for cross-service and cross-domain verification: any of N services verifies a JWT locally with zero calls to a central store, which matters for microservice fan-out and multi-backend mobile/SPA clients -- not because Redis-backed sessions can't handle raw QPS to a single service.

flashcards.q: What should you NOT put in a JWT's claims, and why?
flashcards.a: Fast-changing permissions (a revocation won't take effect until the token expires) or large data sets (bloats the token sent on every request, can hit header-size limits). Keep to sub, exp, and a small number of coarse, slow-changing claims like role or tenant ID.

flashcards.q: What is OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection (RFC 7662) and when does it beat the local-JWT-plus-refresh hybrid?
flashcards.a: A protocol where verification is a network call to the authorization server (cacheable at the edge) rather than local signature checking. It wins when resource servers don't hold/trust the verification key material, or when centralized real-time visibility into every token check is required for compliance.
